title: Towards a Sustainable Indoor Lighting Design: Effects of Artificial Light on the Emotional State of Adolescents in the Classroom
central_proposition: Current LED lighting design, particularly in educational settings, often disregards the non-visual effects of light on human circadian rhythms and emotional states, necessitating new regulations and a shift towards lighting designs that mimic natural light cycles for adolescent health and well-being.

concept_definitions.name: Chronobiology
concept_definitions.definition: the branch of science that deals with the physiological variations of living beings called circadian rhythms, which occur approximately every 24 h, as well as the study of the processes of synchronization with the surrounding environment

concept_definitions.name: Chronotype
concept_definitions.definition: The variation of endogenous circadian rhythms that are determined from individual differences and psychological factors

concept_definitions.name: Chronodisruption (CD)
concept_definitions.definition: an alteration in the internal temporal order of physiological, biological, and behavioral rhythms. If chronodisruption becomes chronic, the asynchrony, advancement, or retardation of peripheral clocks may occur

concept_definitions.name: Photohygiene
concept_definitions.definition: exposure to light under the optimal conditions of periodicity, quality, and quantity

concept_definitions.name: Dim light melatonin onset (DLMO)
concept_definitions.definition: refers to the onset of melatonin secretion under low light conditions. The human body is programmed for this moment to occur when the sun is setting.

concept_definitions.name: Electroluminescence
concept_definitions.definition: The light emission is obtained by the interaction of an electric field with the solid material.

concept_definitions.name: Daylight autonomy (DA)
concept_definitions.definition: sets an illumination value to guarantee autonomy to work only with daylight

concept_definitions.name: Useful daylight illuminance (UDI)
concept_definitions.definition: defines a range of illuminances that can be said to constitute useful levels of illumination

concept_definitions.name: Daylight factor (DF)
concept_definitions.definition: DF = Ei/Eo × 100(%), where Ei = indoor illuminance, Eo = outdoor illuminance (varies from 20-130 klx), and DF = daylight factor.

concept_definitions.name: Temporal light modulation (TLM)
concept_definitions.definition: Current lighting systems vary widely in that their light output shows temporary variations or flickering

argument_structure: The paper establishes the biological basis of human circadian rhythms and their evolution under natural light-dark cycles. It then highlights how modern artificial lighting, especially LEDs and electronic screens, disrupts these natural patterns. A comprehensive review of scientific evidence is presented, detailing the non-visual effects of light (blue light, light at night) on melatonin suppression, sleep quality, mood, cognitive function, and various health outcomes. The paper analyzes the irradiance levels of different light sources and their potential photobiological risks, with a specific focus on adolescents and classroom environments, noting the prevalence of electronic device use and the impact of lighting on student performance and myopia. Finally, it argues for the imperative need for new regulations and lighting design principles that integrate photobiological knowledge to optimize adolescent health and well-being.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The core causal mechanism involves the non-visual effects of light, primarily mediated by intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) in the retina, which are most sensitive to blue light (around 480 nm). Light absorption by ipRGCs, especially at night, suppresses melatonin secretion from the pineal gland, leading to circadian rhythm disruption. This chronodisruption then cascades into negative physiological and psychological consequences, including sleep disturbances, reduced alertness, altered mood, cognitive impairment, and increased risk of metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, and certain cancers. Light exposure can also activate separate mechanisms, influencing alertness through cortisol secretion. In educational settings, poor lighting (inadequate, excessive, or inappropriate spectral composition) negatively impacts visual comfort, attention, mood, and ultimately, student performance and health, such as myopia.

findings.antecedent: Maintaining proper lighting cycles (appropriate levels of light during the day and darkness at night)
findings.mechanism: Biological clocks in living organisms are adapted to periodic light-dark cycles, and proper lighting cycles help synchronize these internal clocks.
findings.quote: Maintaining proper lighting cycles, with appropriate levels of light during the day and darkness at night is beneficial to the synchronization of the circadian system.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to light at night (LAN), particularly at short wavelengths (blue light)
findings.mechanism: The best-known pathway is related to the regulation of melatonin secretions by the pineal gland, where light at night suppresses melatonin.
findings.quote: Exposure to light at night, particularly at short wavelengths, suppresses melatonin and influences insomnia.

findings.mechanism: Light activates a mechanism separate from that of melatonin suppression, during which cortisol is secreted.
findings.quote: The other pathway acts on the level of alertness by activating a mechanism separate from that of melatonin suppression, during which cortisol is secreted [21].

findings.consequent: Negative effects on sleep structure and quality
findings.mechanism: Disruption of natural light-dark cycles by artificial light.
findings.quote: A study carried out by Cho et al. [24] stated that sleeping with the lights on causes acute negative effects on the structure and quality of sleep.

findings.antecedent: Chronodisruption produced by artificial light during the night
findings.consequent: Increased incidence of metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, cognitive and affective disorders
findings.mechanism: Alteration in the internal temporal order of physiological, biological, and behavioral rhythms.
findings.quote: Epidemiological, clinical, and experimental studies with animal models show that the chronodisruption produced by artificial light during the night may be related to pathologies such as the increased incidence of metabolic syndrome [29], cardiovascular disease [29], and cognitive and affective disorders [30].

findings.antecedent: Exposure to bright white or high blue light
findings.mechanism: Light, particularly blue light, stimulates non-visual photoreceptors (ipRGCs) which influence alertness pathways.
findings.quote: Recent research has shown that exposure to bright white or high blue light stimulates alertness...

findings.mechanism: Sunlight helps align internal circadian rhythms, bringing melatonin release closer to sunset and elimination closer to dawn.
findings.quote: In their conclusions they state that “increased exposure to sunlight may help reduce the health consequences of circadian disruption”.

findings.antecedent: Level of ambient light in the room during sleep period
findings.consequent: Other diseases such as diabetes, obesity, depression, and affective disorders
findings.mechanism: Light at night disrupts circadian rhythms and melatonin production, which are linked to various physiological and psychological processes.
findings.quote: Stevens claims that the level of ambient light in the room during the sleep period is associated with other diseases such as diabetes, obesity, depression, and affective disorders, supported by multiple publications...

findings.consequent: Oxidative stress and reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation in retinal cells
findings.mechanism: Blue light, especially at high intensities, can induce oxidative damage in the retina.
findings.quote: Torkaz et al. [50] (2013) stated that the retina is especially exposed to oxidative stress due to high oxygen pressure, UV exposure, and blue light promoting the generation of ROS.

findings.antecedent: Low indoor lighting and natural light
findings.consequent: Increase in myopia among children and adolescents
findings.mechanism: The specific causes are unknown, but a lack of natural light exposure is a suspected factor.
findings.quote: There is an increasing number of publications by researchers (mainly from Asian countries) that relate low indoor lighting and natural light to the increase in myopia among children and adolescents worldwide...

findings.antecedent: Students exposed to more natural light (daylight) in classrooms
findings.consequent: Better reading and math test scores
findings.mechanism: Natural light positively influences student performance, potentially through improved visual comfort, mood, and circadian entrainment.
findings.quote: Students exposed to more natural light (i.e., daylight) in their classrooms perform better than students exposed to less natural light [94].

findings.antecedent: Poor lighting (inadequate or excessive, or inappropriate spectral composition) in classrooms
findings.consequent: Negative effects on children's performance and mood
findings.mechanism: Poor lighting can lead to visual discomfort, headaches, fixation problems, and disrupt biorhythms, impacting cognitive function and emotional state.
findings.quote: Some authors have realized, from the results of their studies, that poor lighting, whether natural or artificial, has notable negative effects on children's performance and mood [84,85].

findings.antecedent: New LED luminaires (with customizable spectral composition, especially blue light intensity)
findings.consequent: Influence on the "mood" of affected people (adolescents)
findings.mechanism: The ability to increase blue light intensity without increasing illuminance allows for manipulation of light's non-visual effects on circadian rhythms and neuromodulatory systems that affect mood.
findings.quote: The new generation of LED lights whose blue light intensity can be increased without increasing the illuminance, makes it possible for the professionals responsible for educational centers to recognize and alter the composition of their centers' lights since this composition can influence the "mood" of the affected people, including adolescents.

findings.mechanism: ALAN disrupts the natural light-dark cycle, interfering with the body's internal clocks.
findings.quote: Artificial light at night (ALAN) is drawing the attention of researchers and environmentalists for its ever-increasing evidence on its capacity for “desynchronization” of organismal physiology [32].

findings.consequent: Delay in transition from serotonin to melatonin and rest process
findings.mechanism: Even small amounts of light at night can suppress melatonin, which is essential for initiating rest.
findings.quote: The current majority of studies states that the minimum amount of light that we receive from 9:00-10:00 p.m. will delay the transition from serotonin to melatonin and, therefore, delay the process of rest that is essential for health.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Implementing dynamic LED lighting in classrooms that mimics natural daylight cycles (higher blue in day, lower blue at night) will improve adolescent sleep quality and reduce chronodisruption compared to static, high-CCT LED lighting.

Adolescents exposed to classroom lighting with spectral compositions closer to natural sunlight will exhibit better academic performance and more positive emotional states than those exposed to conventional artificial lighting.

Educational interventions promoting 'photohygiene' (optimal light exposure periodicity, quality, and quantity) among adolescents will lead to improved sleep, reduced incidence of mood disorders, and better academic outcomes.

The development and implementation of specific regulations for the spectral composition and irradiance of LED luminaires in educational and residential settings will mitigate the negative non-visual health effects on adolescents.

Monitoring the blue light component of indoor lighting in schools will reveal a correlation between higher blue light exposure at inappropriate times and increased reports of sleep disturbances or mood issues among students.
bridge_warrants: The paper connects the biological evolution of humans under natural light cycles to the modern disruption caused by artificial light, bridging evolutionary biology with contemporary environmental design.

It links the physiological mechanisms of melatonin suppression and cortisol secretion to broader health outcomes like metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, and cognitive disorders, emphasizing the systemic impact of light.
It highlights the need to integrate photobiological knowledge into architectural lighting design, bridging science with design practice.
methodological_critiques: Scarcity of existing research on the systemic effects of continuously varying blue light percentage, especially in children and adolescents, due to the novelty of alterable LED components.
Lack of regulatory control over the spectral composition of commercially available LED luminaires and the absence of legislation on non-visual effects of light.
No specific publications found on the composition of light in adolescent training centers or the psychological responses to it.

Existing studies on blue light damage to living tissue often use monochromatic LEDs at much higher irradiances than electronic devices, and employ nocturnal animal models (mice, rabbits) whose visual systems are more sensitive to light than humans, making direct transposition of results to humans problematic.
model_structure: The paper implicitly proposes a model where environmental light input (natural and artificial, with varying spectral compositions and intensities) is processed by the human visual system (including ipRGCs). This processing influences chronobiological regulation (melatonin and cortisol secretion), which in turn either entrains or disrupts circadian rhythms. Entrained rhythms lead to positive physiological and psychological outcomes (good sleep, alertness, positive mood, cognitive performance), while disrupted rhythms (chronodisruption) lead to negative outcomes (sleep disturbances, reduced alertness, negative mood, cognitive impairment, and increased risk of various health pathologies like metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, certain cancers, and myopia). This model implies a feedback loop where awareness of these effects should drive improved lighting design and regulation.
limitations: Scarcity of existing research on the systemic effects of continuously varying blue light percentage, especially in children and adolescents, due to the novelty of alterable LED components.
Lack of regulatory control over the spectral composition of commercially available LED luminaires and the absence of legislation on non-visual effects of light.
No specific publications found on the composition of light in adolescent training centers or the psychological responses to it.
Methodological limitations in existing studies on blue light damage to living tissue (e.g., use of monochromatic LEDs at much higher irradiances, nocturnal animal models).

paper_metadata.title: Incandescent Affect: Turning on the Hot Emotional System With Bright Light
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Incandescent affect: Turning on the hot emotional system with bright light
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: AbstractWe propose that turning on the light can turn on the hot emotional system. Across six studies we show that ambient brightness makes people feel warmer, which increases the intensity of their affective response, including sensation seeking from spicy‐hot foods, perception of aggression and sexiness (“hotness”) in others, and generating more extreme affective reactions toward positive and negative words and drinks. We suggest that these effects arise because light underlies perception of heat, and perception of heat can trigger the hot emotional system. Thus, turning down the light, effortless and unassuming as it may seem, can reduce emotionality in everyday decisions, most of which take place under bright light.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Light exposure, particularly its timing and spectral composition, regulates the human circadian system, influencing physiological and psychological states.

Light influences human physiology and psychology (e.g., mood, alertness, cognition) through pathways independent of conscious vision, primarily via intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs).

mechanism_chain.description: The paper synthesizes how artificial light characteristics influence emotional states in adolescents through the circadian system.

steps.to_construct: Activation of intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs)
Regulation of melatonin secretion and circadian rhythm synchronization
